newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Plans for Yugo capital market premature - experts.
newsitem.headline: Plans for Yugo capital market premature - experts.

text.p: Economists said on Friday plans by the Yugoslav government to push companies and banks into selling stocks on the bourse would fail due to a lack of basic market institutions.
The Yugoslav Securities Commission (YSC), anxious to create a capital market, has urged companies and banks to begin trading stocks on the country's bourse.
The YSC has warned firms that an entire share issue has to be sold -- either on the bourse or directly to other companies -- to be considered legal.
But traders and analysts said the YSC campaign was unrealistic and said the economy required genuine mass privatisation, free market reforms and stability before a capital market could take shape.

"We need investment banks, investment funds, rating agencies and strong managerial teams to introduce the household sector to the market and provide top risk management," said Stojan Dabic, head of the Financial Market Development Centre.
Real investment banking that would win the trust of local investors could be established only with the help of foreign banks, Dabic, who created the Belgrade bourse, told Reuters.

The public lost trust in the financial system after a devastating bout of hyperinflation in 1993, which reached 60 percent a day. Authorities froze indefinitely some 6.6 billion German marks in hard currency savings.
According to some estimates, people in rump Yugoslavia keep some 3-5 billion German marks "under their mattresses".
Economists said the fact that 50 percent of the total money supply fell outside the banking system only confirmed deep distrust in the country's financial institutions.
The M1 money supply stood at 4.485 billion dinars at the end of August.
Once the financial market infrastructure is built and trust regained, the securities commission can expect more success, analysts said.
Until then, statements released by the YSC would not be sufficient to encourage trading on the bourse.
"The YSC has every right to strengthen criteria to protect investors. But so far, the practice was too liberal," Bosko Zivkovic of the private CES-Mecon economic institute said.
"In theory, it is possible to sell a new share issue on the bourse. But it is an illusion to insist on it," Zivkovic said.
Currently, banks and companies mainly raise capital by selling shares directly to one another, with no individuals participating.
Owning a share in a bank does not bring a dividend or capital gain. "Who wants to own shares of a ruined bank?" an analyst who asked not to be named said.

"If I wanted to sell shares on the bourse, they would maybe fetch 20 percent of their face value. But in that case, I would be accused of selling off socially-owned capital for nothing," another analyst said.
Analysts also said the value of bank shares does not reflect the poor state of the banking sector and the structure of its capital.
Despite ambitious statements from the YSC, analysts said it has sometimes failed to live up to its own regulations, issuing licenses to insolvent companies.
"Known buyers never bought shares of their choice. They were offered 'junk'. Fortunately, the damage was not as large because shares were never sold on the bourse," an analyst said.
YSC officials were unavailable for comment. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
